source.title: One axis and two features, how I solved the first puzzle from BlueDot and how a classifier hid country on the food direction

page_placements.theme: Multidimensional subspaces, structured feature families and nonlinear codes

record.tranche_reason: The post measures feature geometry in a trained classifier using probes and quadratic analysis, rather than reproducing the original toy-model method.
record.gate_note: Reports measurements of country and food representations sharing a direction, plus geometry from adversarially trained representations. The Boolean-pair result is reported only as the best match across 63 tests; individual pair scores are not separately recorded here. Probe scores used to identify the country feature and characterize its geometry are included; no cited results from other work are used as findings.
record.test_reason: The post analyses one puzzle classifier that encodes 8 binary features in a 64-dimensional layer, so there are far fewer features than dimensions. It finds that country is read as the squared projection onto the food direction. That is a nonlinear readout of one feature from another feature's direction. It is not superposition of many sparse features under capacity pressure, and it does not test 1-D versus multi-dimensional features. The puzzle model was likely built to hide country, and Experiments A and B induce the hiding on purpose with adversarial training. The post calls the result superposition but never measures capacity, sparsity or feature counts, so the findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is mostly right. The authors conclude that the classifier reuses the food axis for country, reading food by the sign and country by the magnitude of the projection. They conclude that linear probes can miss features, that adversarial training can hide a feature from linear readout, and that superposition arises under dimensionality pressure. That last point is asserted, not tested.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a trained text classifier and activation probes, quadratic geometry analysis, and adversarial training; it does not reproduce the original toy-model setup or method.
record.method_sensitivity: The learned geometry differs across the original classifier and adversarially trained Experiments A and B; the added shape loss in Experiment B changes the linear country AUC and the reported geometry.

fits_no_version.finding: In a puzzle classifier, country has no linear direction (linear AUC 0.487) but is read as the squared projection onto the food direction (AUC 0.976). Food and country labels are independent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A network can store two independent binary features on one direction using different readouts (sign versus magnitude), which hides one of them from linear probes.

fits_no_version.finding: A single centroid gives chance accuracy (0.495), and vector norm gives only an inverted, partial signal (AUC 0.21, or 0.79 inverted).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this classifier, country information is not captured by one centroid or by global vector norm alone.

fits_no_version.finding: Gradient-reversal training cut linear country AUC to 0.519 (0.650 with a shape loss) while the MLP probe AUC stayed at 0.974.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial training can make a feature linearly undecodable while keeping it nonlinearly decodable, and a prescribed shape loss only partly steers the geometry.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. The evidence is from one small classifier and the post does not establish that a capacity constraint caused the observed feature sharing. Some conclusions rely on probe-based inferences and reported geometry rather than a controlled comparison of feature dimensionality.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No toy setting with more sparse features than dimensions, no sparsity sweep, no geometry of many features.
No manipulation of capacity or feature importance. The closing claim about dimensionality pressure is asserted, not measured.
No test of what causes direction sharing; 8 features in 64 dims is not examined as a no-capacity-pressure case.
No comparison of one-dimensional versus multi-dimensional superposed features.

record.verdict_notes: This is a blog post on a BlueDot puzzle; the puzzle model was probably constructed to hide country. Only 8 features sit in 64 dimensions, so the case does not match the claim's capacity-driven superposition, despite the author's label. There is one model, no uncertainty estimates, and no controls on capacity.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry.
Does not test whether limited capacity causes polysemanticity or whether importance determines which features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not establish that polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure or test alternative causes of it.
The subject is a small text classifier, not an LLM; no LLM feature-spreading or SAE results are reported.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Shows a particular two-feature, one-axis case and separately trained country representations; does not systematically compare one- versus multi-dimensional superposed features across models.

relation.reason: The post describes shared-axis nonlinear encoding as superposition, but does not test capacity-driven overlapping linear representations or use that finding as a tool.

tranche.reason: The results concern nonlinear feature readout and deliberately induced concealment from linear probes. They do not test the catalog's superposition versions; dimensionality pressure is asserted without being experimentally tested.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased. Experiment B's two droplets are a training target that failed to emerge; its linear concealment is weaker than Experiment A's.
